Learning Objectives
Review factors that influence recovery after trauma.
Explain why informed patients are more likely to adhere to treatment recommendations,
report satisfaction with their care, and have better functional outcomes.
Review social determinants of health that may increase the risk of prolonged or incomplete
recovery.
Explain the effects of trauma on mental health.
Discuss the effects of psychosocial programming and education after trauma.
Review factors that contribute to physician burnout and methods to attain better work-life
balance.

Introduction
A biopsychosocial model encompasses domains related to recovery and long-term outcomes
after trauma.
Pre-injury psychiatric illness, substance abuse, limited social support, lower education levels,
low self-efficacy, and limited coping skills portend limitations after major injury.

Introduction
Recovery after trauma is influenced by biologic, psychological, and social factors.
Traditionally, orthopaedic surgeons have functioned in a multidisciplinary capacity
alongside colleagues in related surgical disciplines and rehabilitation; therefore, they
may have little to no consideration for issues outside of the injury. However, baseline
psychosocial status influences the risks for trauma and optimal recovery. Trauma is the
leading cause of death and disability among individuals younger than 45 years and
clearly affects life after the initial injury episode and related hospitalization. The annual
economic burden of trauma in the United States outweighs the costs of cardiovascular,
cerebrovascular, and cancer care combined, primarily because of the lasting effects of
injury on the indirect costs of lost workplace productivity for patients and their
caregivers. Chronic pain, mental illness, and adverse social circumstances predispose
patients to poor outcomes.1-6
A growing body of evidence supports the assertion that physical function and patient-
reported outcomes are related to mental and social health, with respective risk and
protective factors.7,8 Within this framework, interventions to improve patient education,
engagement, and self-efficacy may enhance the magnitude and efficiency of recovery.9-
11 Such interventions are termed trauma-informed care.
Unique Role of the Caregiver
Traumatologists are in a position to mitigate morbidity after injury via provisional and
definitive fracture care and posttraumatic reconstruction. Patient engagement and education

by the treating surgeon and team improve patient and provider satisfaction.
Compassion is empathy combined with a desire to alleviate the burden of injury. Beyond the
surgical and procedural aspects of care, a surgeon can offer compassion in communication to
enable care of the entire patient.

Unique Role of the Caregiver
Self-efficacy represents an individual’s belief that he or she can manage given
circumstances. Resilience is the ability to emotionally cope with adversity. Although
baseline self-efficacy and resilience confer patient advantages along the recovery
pathway, trust in physicians and other care providers facilitates patient engagement with
available resources and promotes recovery and the development of additional
resilience. Trust builds hope. Listening actively, conveying compassion, and maintaining
objectivity without predisposition or judgment may be a challenge for surgeons but are
worthy goals for patient relationships.12 They are core elements of a trauma-informed
approach.
Informed, educated patients are more likely to adhere to treatment recommendations,
are more likely to report satisfaction with their care, and have better functional
outcomes after injury.3,4,13-16 Patient recall after injury is poor, likely limited by factors
such as severe pain, head injury, intoxication, medication, and stress; however,
educational materials and interventions may enhance patient knowledge about injury
and recovery, improving engagement and potentially reducing complications.17-19
Involving patients in their care and connecting them with providers in other disciplines, if
appropriate, promote self-efficacy and resilience. Continuous reassessment of patient
progress on the recovery pathway will reveal opportunities for encouragement and
redirection. The longevity of such relationships can create a greater sense of provider
satisfaction, despite the residual physical limitations that may affect trauma patients.
Key Elements of Recovery

Key Elements of Recovery
Pain is worsened by anxiety and, in combination with anxiety and depression, may foster
catastrophizing and protracted recovery, with poor long-term outcomes.4,22,23 Early
strategies to manage pain include setting expectations and providing education. The
implementation of preemptive analgesia reduces the severity of perceived pain.24
Multimodal pain management may block multiple steps along the pain cascade and has
been associated with lower opioid use, better patient-reported outcomes, and increased
satisfaction with pain management.25,26 Alternative therapies, including counseling,
aromatherapy, cryotherapy, and other nontraditional modalities, also may be
effective.2,25,27
Psychological Aspects of Recovery
Identifying underlying mental illness and new mental illness
Many trauma patients have preexisting mental illness. Often, such illness is not identified or
managed in the acute trauma setting.
Mental health worsens after trauma. Anxiety, depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder
(PTSD) are the most frequent new diagnoses.
Mental illness is associated with pain and poor patient-reported functional outcomes.

Psychological Aspects of Recovery

Preexisting mental illness is common among trauma patients and is exacerbated by new
injury. Orthopaedic surgeons often fail to identify and manage preexisting mental
illness.28 Mental health issues occur in as many as one-half of patients after trauma, with
depression being the most frequent issue.28-32 After major trauma, some surgeons
argue that all survivors experience an adjustment disorder at a minimum. Anxiety and
PTSD also are common.2,32-36 Patients who are assaulted, especially if the assault
involves a shooting, have a higher risk for PTSD.31,35,37 A recent study noted that PTSD
was 13 times more likely to develop in patients who had a fear of death from their
injury.38 In trauma patients, mental illness is associated with higher levels of reported
pain, increased opioid consumption, a risk of catastrophizing, and poor patient
satisfaction and outcomes.2-4,14-16,26,29,39 In addition, patients who are debilitated by
mental illness have a lower likelihood of adherence to treatment recommendations,
more frequent postoperative complications, and higher rates of trauma
recidivism.28,33,40
Screening for mental illness is indicated after trauma and is supported by recent
appropriate use criteria and clinical practice guidelines.41,42 The evaluation of mental
health, social support, and stressors and an assessment of baseline coping ability and
resilience are beneficial, even in patients deemed have a lower risk for poor
outcomes.34,43,44 Psychosocial risk factors for poor outcomes include pre-injury
psychiatric conditions and severe musculoskeletal injury with long-term major functional
limitations. Protective factors include baseline social support systems, self-efficacy, and
higher educational levels.8,23,41
Substance Use and Abuse
Tobacco use is common among trauma patients and is associated with increased pain and
poorer patient-reported functional outcomes after trauma.
Alcohol misuse is common among trauma patients, ranging from episodic intoxication or
binge drinking to alcohol abuse and alcohol dependence (defined as abuse with tolerance and
withdrawal phenomena).
Recreational drug use is associated with increased pain and increased opioid consumption
after trauma.


Substance Use and Abuse
Trauma patients are more likely to be tobacco users.6 Tobacco users report increased
pain and have been shown to have increased opioid consumption after injury.1,28,45
They also have been noted to have a protracted recovery and poorer late functional
outcomes.5,6,29 These consequences may result from poor baseline musculoskeletal
health and/or an altered biochemical response to pain. Periods of tobacco cessation,
even perioperatively, have been associated with better pulmonary function and a
decreased risk for infection.46
Alcohol misuse also is pervasive among trauma patients. Alcohol misuse likely is
underdiagnosed and underreported. Alcohol abuse usually is associated with chronic
malnutrition because of impaired hepatic synthetic function and poor protein and
vitamin dietary intake, resulting in higher rates of wound healing problems, infection,
and fracture nonunion.29,47 Recreational drug use is associated with increased opioid
consumption after injury and predisposes patients to catastrophizing. Recreational drug
use also is associated with poorer patient-reported functional outcomes and an
increased risk for trauma recidivism.1,5,29,40,48
Social Aspects of Recovery
Social determinants of health (SDOHs) and other patient and injury factors may pose risks for
prolonged and/or incomplete recovery.
Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are traumatic events or environmental circumstances
occurring before age 18 years that increase the risk for chronic health conditions and poor
socioeconomic status.

Social Aspects of Recovery
SDOHs are conditions in the environment (home, work, school, community, etc.) that
influence risks and outcomes. Physical, social, and economic aspects in the environment
and patterns of well-being and social engagement are considered. Five key areas of
SDOHs have been identified.49,50
Optimizing education and resources that address deficiencies within the SDOHs may
improve physical and mental health, well-being, and quality of life.
Most adults have experienced at least one ACE, and women and some minority groups
have an increased risk for additional ACEs. Violence, abuse, and neglect are ACEs that
may be experienced and/or witnessed. Household instability, including parental absence
or separation; mental health problems; and substance abuse in the environment are
common ACEs. Children growing up with ACEs and associated issues, such as food or
housing insecurity, often experience frequent, prolonged stress, known as toxic stress,
which may adversely affect attention, learning, and mental and physical health. A higher
number of ACEs and a longer length of exposure are directly related to higher risks for
anxiety, depression, substance abuse, and suicide.49 These conditions affect injury and
recovery in trauma patients.
Optimizing Recovery After Trauma
Physical
Traditional surgical education equips physicians in the diagnosis and management of
musculoskeletal conditions, including an array of musculoskeletal injuries.
The optimization of the mental and social conditions specific to a patient enhances physical
recovery by accelerating the timeline and enhancing its full potential.8,9,16,51-56
Effective pain management and mitigation are key elements of recovery.
Pain
Multimodal pain management decreases narcotic consumption and reduces pain.

Pain catastrophizing is defined as a magnification of the threat of pain and a sense of
helplessness around pain.
Psychological
Resources and strategies to improve mental health are effective in decreasing the risk for
new or exacerbated mental illness after trauma.
Engagement of providers with expertise in recovery coaching and counseling improves
patient engagement and satisfaction and reduces mental illness.
Biopsychosocial interventions, including mindfulness, relaxation, and coping mechanisms,
are helpful techniques to reduce anxiety and pain.
Social
Identify and engage support persons.
Mitigate risk factors.
Provide resources and strategies.

Optimizing Recovery After Trauma
The initial management of pain should include education and the setting of
expectations.25,27,51 This stage includes education about the injury and about the
anticipated treatment and recovery. Education reduces anxiety, and anxiety is associated
with a heightened pain response. Inadequately managed pain fosters catastrophizing
and mental illness and has a detrimental effect on outcomes.1-4,8,22,24,29,48 Multimodal
pain management that incorporates medications and delivery pathways is associated
with decreased reported pain and decreased narcotic consumption. Less inpatient
narcotic use and more modest discharge prescriptions are associated with decreased
post-discharge opioid use.45 Regional anesthesia is an effective adjunct to postoperative
pain management, particularly in assessing the risk for compartment syndrome. The use
of various nonnarcotic medications, such as NSAIDs, gabapentinoids, and
acetaminophen, in addition to small doses of short-acting opioids is encouraged.27
Adverse effects related to opioids also are mitigated. Alternative therapies, including
cryotherapy, aromatherapy, and biofeedback techniques, also are effective for acute or
chronic pain.

Baseline chronic pain managed via prescription and/or recreational substances is
common in trauma patients.4,26 Early identification and management, incorporating
pain management and the services of addiction experts, may be paramount in
optimizing recovery.
Programs have been developed to provide patient and family education and to foster
the engagement of patients and their support systems after trauma. The Trauma
Survivors Network was created to provide education and support, and initial results have
been promising.8,9,16,23,52,53 Central to the Trauma Survivors Network is the concept of
peer support rather than professional support. Peer mentorship that involves prior
trauma patients as mentors for new trauma patients enables the survivorship of trauma
and promotes social connectedness, self-efficacy, and resilience.16 Recent evidence
shows that patients engaged in psychosocial programming and educational
interventions after trauma have lower rates of new or worsening mental illness.54,55 A
better adherence to treatment recommendations also is observed.56
Social needs after injury may encompass transportation, housing, vocational support,
durable medical equipment, and various other items and services unique to the injured
person, their social support system, and their recovery timeline. Social workers and case
managers traditionally work alongside treating physicians and therapists in identifying
specific needs and facilitating the transition to home.
Trauma Surgeon Wellness
Surgeon self-awareness and self-care are necessary to provide effective care for others. For
surgeons, the two most important risks to health and well-being are burnout and moral injury.
Burnout definition
Burnout is characterized by emotional exhaustion, a reduced sense of personal
accomplishment, and depersonalization.
The Physician Well-Being Index and the Maslach Burnout Inventory are related assessments
for providers.
Burnout should not be perceived as a failure of individual resilience.

Moral injury definition
Moral injury is defined as a failure to adequately provide for patient needs or a failure to
provide quality care for any reason on the part of the provider, a colleague, or the system.
Conflict between physician allegiance to the patient and the healthcare system may foster
moral injury.
Work-life balance

Trauma Surgeon Wellness
In recent surveys, as many as 61% of trauma surgeons reported burnout.57,58 Several
factors have been associated with burnout, including being in the mid-career stage,
spending more hours at work, spending fewer hours at home, and feeling that a better
job may exist.58,59 An improved sense of time management decreases the risk of
burnout, which is associated with depression, substance abuse, and suicide.60-62
Burnout also is associated with decreased patient satisfaction scores and a higher risk
for medical errors and malpractice.57,60
Debate exists regarding the definitions of moral injury and burnout and their
relationships.63,64 Moral injury, an inability to adequately provide high-quality care
because of system challenges, may contribute to physician burnout. Physician advocacy
and empowerment in the workplace improve morale and enhance patient care and
experience. The Institute for Healthcare Improvement Triple Aim is a means of
optimizing healthcare system performance by improving population health, enhancing
the patient experience, and reducing the costs of care. Ironically, the inability to achieve
progress in these areas may promote a sense of moral injury. Recently, a fourth aim was
added (the Quadruple Aim) to include improving the work life of clinicians and staff.65
The fourth aim may be achieved via physician empowerment and team efforts to foster
greater control over the work environment. It also may include resources or processes to
promote better physician self-care and well-being.64,65 Physician peer mentorship may
be helpful.
Work-life balance offsets time spent in work responsibilities with time spent in personal,
family, and avocational and recreational activities. Physicians who self-report better

work-life balance have a lower risk for burnout.58 Factors associated with a better work-

Leadership initiatives to engage physicians and promote flexibility in the workplace to
encourage self-care have been viewed positively and represent novel methods that
warrant additional research and adoption.68,69
Summary

Summary
Physical function and patient-reported outcomes after trauma are related to mental and
social health. Risk factors for poor outcomes include baseline chronic pain, substance
abuse, other mental illness, ACEs, and deficiencies in SDOHs. Protective factors include
social support, self-efficacy, and higher educational levels. Psychosocial interventions
and patient education improve engagement, self-efficacy, and patient satisfaction with
care. These interventions also may enhance the magnitude and efficiency of recovery.
Physicians are affected increasingly by moral injury and burnout. Factors associated with
a better work-life balance may decrease the risk for burnout. Healthcare leadership
initiatives to promote workplace flexibility and to advocate on behalf of surgeons may
mitigate moral injury.
